Glossary — every term, simply Patta land Land for which a private owner holds a government-issued title record. Example: an ordinary farmer with a clean revenue record along the Musi’s middle reaches is a patta landowner under this scheme. Buffer zone A protective strip of land just outside a water body’s Full Tank Level, kept free of construction to protect its ecology and absorb flood flow. Example: land here gets 800 sq yards/acre under today’s scheme, less than ordinary patta land further from the river. Full Tank Level (FTL) The highest water level a lake or river stretch is engineered to hold. Example: land inside this line is legally meant to stay open for water, which is why its pooling return (400 sq yards/acre) is the smallest among patta categories. Encroachment land Land occupied or built on without a valid title, often riverbed or government land settled informally over time. Example: occupants here get 300 sq yards/acre — something, but the least of any category, reflecting their weaker legal claim. Transferable Development Rights (TDR) A certificate given to a landowner who surrenders land, letting them build extra floor area on a different plot they own, or sell that right to someone else (often a builder) instead of taking cash or a returned plot. Example: a buffer-zone owner here can choose TDR instead of the 800 sq-yard allotment. Land pooling vs. land acquisition Acquisition takes your land and pays fixed compensation under law; pooling takes your land TEMPORARILY, develops the whole area with roads and services, and gives you back a smaller, serviced plot from the same pooled land — the return ratio is set by whichever order governs that specific project, not by one universal rule. Example: today’s Musi ratios are one such project-specific pooling order, distinct from HMDA’s separate 60:40 one. 60:40 land-pooling ratio (HMDA) HMDA’s own standard scheme returns landowners roughly 60% of the value created (in practice, cited elsewhere as around 1,741 sq yards of developed plot per acre pooled), keeping 40% to sell and fund infrastructure. Example: this is the benchmark today’s Musi scheme is explicitly reported as NOT following. Multiple Use Zone A Master Plan land-use tag permitting a mix of residential, commercial and other uses on one parcel, rather than restricting it to a single use. Example: plots returned under this scheme carry this tag, which generally helps resale value and future construction flexibility. Master Plan A local or metropolitan authority’s official, legally-binding zoning map and rulebook, setting out what each area of land may be used for. Example: the "Multiple Use Zone" classification above is a Master Plan designation. Change-of-land-use (CLU) / land-use conversion charge A fee payable when a parcel’s officially recorded use (e.g. agricultural) is formally changed to another use (e.g. residential/commercial). Example: today’s scheme has the implementing entity, not the landowner, bear this charge on the plots handed back. Nala A natural or man-made storm-water drainage channel. Example: "nala charges" in this scheme relate to drainage-related costs on patta land, which the implementing entity is absorbing rather than passing to owners. Stamp duty A state tax paid on registering a property transaction, usually calculated as a percentage of the property’s market value. Example: Telangana’s normal combined stamp duty and registration charge runs close to 6% on an ordinary sale; this scheme fixes it at just 0.5% for plots returned to landowners — a real, quantifiable sweetener. 2026-10-01|ls-patta-2c: 2C patta explained: why assigned land drags buyers into CID cases Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: 2C Assigned Patta Explained: Why This Land Type Lands Buyers in CID Cases — 1acre.in Key Highlights Assigned patta is government WELFARE land with strings attached — strings that survive every deed registered after the original allotment. Restriction periods run 10–20 years by scheme — counted from the ALLOTMENT date, not from when the current seller acquired it. SC/ST-assigned land never loses its restriction. Buyers get pulled into CB-CID cases as often as sellers: registering a deed on restricted land counts as participation, intent or not. IPC 420, 465, 468 and 471 recur in these charge sheets — and 420 is NON-BAILABLE. 2C patta (converted-for-residential land) and assigned patta are DIFFERENT things — agents blur them, and that blur alone has put buyers in front of investigators. The patta’s remarks column and the A-Register hold everything you need — read both before any advance. What assigned patta actually is It reads like any other patta — survey number, name, extent, classification. The difference hides in a clause in the REMARKS section, or in the assignment order sitting behind the patta that sellers do not always show. Governments have allotted land to landless families, SC/ST beneficiaries, ex-servicemen and other eligible groups under welfare schemes — and the original assignment order carries the real terms: how long the beneficiary must hold, what the land may be used for, and whether government approval is needed before any sale. What the conditions mean in practice Restriction periods commonly run 10–20 years depending on the scheme — counted from the DATE OF ALLOTMENT, not from whenever the current seller took over. Violate them and the government cancels the patta and takes the land back — no warning, no compensation. The person who paid full market price is left with nothing, and on record the sale is treated as if it never legally happened. Why purchases turn into CID cases The script is always the same: a seller holds assigned land still inside its restriction period; the buyer is told the patta is clean or the condition “doesn’t apply anymore”; money moves, the deed registers. Then — sometimes years later — a neighbour complains or a revenue officer notices something during routine inspection. The Tahsildar orders an inquiry, confirms the violation, and the case moves to the police — often the CB-CID. The buyer’s registered deed is not a defence; it is EXHIBIT A. The criminal sections that get invoked IPC 420 — cheating by dishonest inducement, up to seven years, and NON-BAILABLE: arrest can precede a magistrate’s order. IPC 465 — forgery, where patta records were altered or a condition quietly omitted. IPC 468 — forgery for the purpose of cheating. IPC 471 — USING a forged document as genuine — the section that can reach a buyer who registered a deed without ever checking its underlying conditions. This is the lesson’s hardest truth: in assigned-land cases the buyer is treated as a participant, not merely a victim. 2C patta ≠ assigned patta 2C patta : agricultural land formally CONVERTED for residential use — its one condition (agricultural classification) already resolved through a conversion order. No welfare distribution behind it, no community restriction, no lock-in on sale. Assigned patta : welfare redistribution, with conditions on who may own, how long they must hold, and whether it can be sold at all. Agents in a hurry blur the two — and that blur alone has put buyers in front of investigators. If a seller says “2C”, verify it is a CONVERSION story, not an ASSIGNMENT story: the paper trail behind each is completely different. Example: A buyer is shown a “2C patta — fully converted, free to sell”. The A-Register extract tells another story: allotted 2011 under a housing scheme to an SC beneficiary — an assignment, restriction unexpired and, being SC-assigned, never expiring. The “conversion” framing was the con. One ₹50 counter application at the revenue office exposed it. How to verify before you pay ☐ Pull the LATEST patta/ownership record from the state portal. ☐ Get the A-REGISTER extract (or state equivalent) at the revenue office — it shows the original allotment date and scheme. ☐ Compute the restriction period from the ALLOTMENT date, not the seller’s purchase date. ☐ SC/ST-assigned? The restriction does not expire — check buyer eligibility before going one step further. ☐ Even past the window, some schemes require written Collector permission before registration — confirm. ☐ Review the ownership history: a pattern of quick, repeated transfers is exactly what CB-CID investigations flag. Quick answers (FAQ) Can assigned patta land be sold legally? Only where the scheme’s conditions allow — restriction expired, permissions obtained, or formal de-restriction granted. The non-alienation period? 10–20 years by scheme, from allotment; perpetual for SC/ST assignments. Why do BUYERS end up in cases? Because registering a deed on restricted land is treated as participation in the violation. If conditions are violated? Cancellation, resumption without compensation — plus the criminal exposure above. Bottom line This is the one land category where a mistake is not just money — it is a charge sheet. The remarks column and the A-Register cost minutes and rupees to read; read them before any advance, and walk away from any seller who resists the reading. For you: Deepens your assigned-land gate with the criminal dimension: in Telangana assembly work, any parcel whose chain touches a government grant gets the allotment-order + A-Register/Dharani-remarks check BEFORE the agreement — because for a professional developer the reputational cost of one CID summons exceeds any parcel’s margin. And police the vocabulary in your own market: brokers saying “converted” when the record says “assigned” are handing you their liability. 2026-10-01|ls-nri-repat: NRI buying land in India: rules and repatriation Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: NRI Buying Land in India: Rules and Repatriation — 1acre.in Key Highlights NRIs purchase residential and commercial property freely — no cap, no RBI approval. Agricultural land, plantations and farmhouses: barred without RBI permission, granted only in exceptional cases. The funding account — NRE/FCNR vs NRO — decides how much of the sale proceeds can later leave India. Two ceilings coexist: USD 1 million per year (general), and a LIFETIME cap of two residential properties for full repatriation of foreign-funded purchases. Inherited farmland can be kept — but sold only to a resident Indian. FEMA violations are punished for real: penalties can reach three times the amount. What NRI purchase covers under FEMA No single rule — it depends entirely on the land’s category. Residential and commercial: open. Agricultural, plantation, farmhouse: RBI-permission territory, rarely granted. OCI cardholders follow broadly the same lines. Definition — FEMA: the Foreign Exchange Management Act — the law governing what non-residents may hold in India and how money crosses the border. Its property rules now live in the Non-debt Instruments Rules, 2019. How the source of funds decides repatriation The question nobody asks until selling: where did the purchase money COME from? NRE/FCNR (foreign currency) funding: full repatriation of proceeds — but only for two residential properties in a lifetime without special approval. NRO funding or Indian income: repatriation capped at USD 1 million per financial year, whatever the property count. Bought while still a resident: the same 1-million-per-year route through an NRO account. The account choice at purchase becomes irreversible history at sale. Repatriating inherited property Allowed — within the same framework: documentary proof of inheritance, taxes settled, the annual limit observed. The paperwork order matters more than the principle. Why agricultural land is a special case NRIs cannot buy it directly; they CAN inherit it — and then may sell only to a resident Indian citizen, never to another NRI or foreigner. Even after a legitimate sale, repatriation follows the standard annual framework. Inherit-only, sell-to-residents-only, repatriate-within-caps: that layered fence is where NRI families stumble years later. How repatriation actually works, step by step 1. Sale proceeds land in an NRO account — the mandatory starting point. 2. File the income-tax return for the sale year. 3. A chartered accountant issues Form 15CB confirming capital-gains tax is paid. 4. Submit Form 15CA online with the sale deed and bank statements. 5. The bank verifies, converts, remits. Not one bank visit — a CA, a bank and the tax department all signing off; budget weeks, not days. Red flags Cash, or any channel outside normal banking — an outright FEMA violation; every rupee must move through banks. Skipped or botched 15CA/15CB filings — transfers block. Farmland bought without approval — regulatory action, penalties up to three times the amount, and directed disposal of the property. Repatriation limits by funding route How the property was funded What can leave India The cap that applies NRE / FCNR (foreign funds) Full sale proceeds Two residential properties per LIFETIME; beyond that, RBI approval NRO account / Indian income Proceeds via NRO USD 1 million per financial year, any property count Bought while a resident Proceeds via NRO USD 1 million per year Inherited property Proceeds via NRO USD 1 million per year + inheritance proof + tax clearance Foreign funding suits a buyer who will sell at most two properties in a lifetime. NRO-funded and inherited assets share the annual cap — spreading sales across financial years is the planning lever. Pre-purchase checklist ☐ The land’s category confirmed — residential/commercial open; agricultural/plantation closed. ☐ Clear records kept of the funding account for every purchase. ☐ NRO + 15CA/15CB machinery started early when a sale approaches. ☐ The annual USD 1 million cap tracked across same-year sales. ☐ A FEMA-qualified advisor before any transaction. Quick answers (FAQ) Can an NRI buy agricultural land? Not without rare RBI permission — inheritance and (from resident specified relatives) gift are the doors. Is there a time limit to repatriate? The practical clock is tax compliance and the annual cap — plan sale-year paperwork in advance. Does the two-property rule apply to everything? Only to full repatriation of foreign-funded RESIDENTIAL purchases; the annual cap governs the rest. Bottom line Consistent rules, unforgiving of shortcuts: category first, funding account second, documentation third. Getting all three right at purchase is cheap; correcting a FEMA violation after is not. For you: NRI buyers are a real slice of the plot market — the developer fluent in their constraints closes them faster. Keep an NRI closing pack (bank-routed trail, TDS guidance, PoA template, mutation help), and never sell anything smelling of farmland to an NRI, however willing. Glossary — every term, simply Section 22-A prohibited list A state-maintained register of survey numbers a sub-registrar must legally refuse to register. Survey number The unique identifier Telangana land records use to track a parcel — but one survey number can cover anywhere from a fraction of an acre to well over a thousand acres and thousands of separate owners, which is exactly why a single error can freeze so many unrelated people's land at once. Blanket survey-number tagging The core technical error behind this entire saga: flagging an ENTIRE survey number as prohibited because a small part of it is genuinely problematic, instead of flagging only the specific problematic sub-plot. Patta land Land for which a private owner holds a government-issued title record — the category Section 22-A is legally meant to exclude, and the category that keeps getting wrongly trapped by it. 2026-10-02|ls-capital-gains: Capital gains tax on agricultural land sale Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: Capital Gains Tax on Agricultural Land Sale in India — 1acre.in Key Highlights Rural agricultural land is NOT a capital asset under Section 2(14)(iii) — its sale attracts no capital gains tax at all. The rural test is mechanical: the nearest municipality’s census population, and aerial distance of 2 / 6 / 8 km. Urban agricultural land is taxed like any property; long-term starts at 24 months. Section 54B exemption needs TWO years of actual farming before sale, reinvestment in farmland within two years, and a three-year lock-in on the new land. Section 50C lets the taxman substitute the stamp-duty value when you sell below it. When the tax applies at all One question decides everything: is the land RURAL or URBAN under the Income Tax Act? Rural agricultural land is excluded from the very definition of a capital asset by Section 2(14)(iii) — no capital asset, no capital gain, nothing to tax. Urban agricultural land gets no carve-out and is taxed like any other asset. Two owners can sell what looks like the same plot and one pays nothing while the other owes tax on the whole gain — purely because of where the land sits. The rural test — mechanical, not agricultural Nothing to do with how the land is farmed; everything to do with location and population. Land is RURAL if it lies outside a municipality or cantonment of 10,000+ people, AND outside these aerial distances from those limits: 2 km where the population is 10,000–1 lakh; 6 km where it is 1–10 lakh; 8 km where it exceeds 10 lakh. Population comes from the last published census; distance is measured AERIALLY — as the crow flies, not as the road winds. Inside the limits = urban agricultural land = taxable. One nuance: the exemption attaches to the LAND — a farmhouse, well or standing trees sold in the same deal are valued and treated separately. Example: Two farmers sell near Hyderabad (population >10 lakh, so the 8 km band applies). One’s land sits 9 km aerially from the municipal limit — rural, gain fully exempt. The other’s sits 7 km out — urban, fully taxable. Same crop, same buyer profile, two kilometres of geometry worth lakhs in tax. The second test: was it actually farmed? Classification decides the tax; CULTIVATION decides whether your claim survives scrutiny. Revenue records carry seasonal cultivation entries — the evidence that agricultural operations actually happened — and Section 54B leans on exactly that record for its two-year farming condition. Land held bare as pure investment is where exemption claims die at assessment. How the gain is computed Sale price minus purchase cost and expenses. Held 24+ months: long-term. The current long-term regime taxes gains at 12.5% without indexation (indexation having been withdrawn for post-July-2024 sales). And Section 50C looms over the price itself: sell below the stamp-duty value and the department can treat THAT value as your deemed sale price, subject to a tolerance margin — the guideline value quietly setting your tax floor. Rural vs urban at a glance Aspect Rural agricultural land Urban agricultural land Capital asset? No — s.2(14)(iii) excludes it Yes Capital gains tax None LTCG/STCG as applicable TDS on sale (194-IA) Expressly excluded 1% at ₹50 lakh+ (resident seller) Exemption routes Not needed 54B (farmland), 54EC (bonds) The exits: 54B and 54EC Section 54B — individuals and HUFs: reinvest the gain in NEW agricultural land within two years, provided the sold land was farmed for the two years before sale; money not yet reinvested by the return-filing date parks in a Capital Gains Account Scheme; the new land locks in for three years — sell early and the exemption unwinds. Section 54EC — the alternative for long-term gains: NHAI/REC/PFC/IRFC bonds within six months (₹50 lakh cap, five-year lock). The taxes that ride alongside TDS: buyers deduct 1% under 194-IA on urban agricultural land at ₹50 lakh+ — rural land is expressly outside the section. NRI sellers: Section 195 instead, at much higher rates — plan with a lower-deduction certificate. 50C: as above, the stamp-value floor. Quick answers (FAQ) Is rural agricultural land exempt? Fully — it is not a capital asset. How is “rural” defined? The census-population + aerial-distance test above. Indexation still available? Not under the current 12.5% regime. Urban land exemptions? 54B with the farming and lock-in conditions; 54EC bonds. TDS on farmland? Urban yes (₹50L+), rural no. Don’t want to buy farmland again? 54EC bonds, or pay the 12.5% and stay liquid. Bottom line Before selling any farmland, establish three things in writing: the aerial distance to the nearest 10,000+ municipality, the census figure that sets the band, and the cultivation record. Those three lines decide whether the tax is zero, exempt-with-conditions, or fully payable — get a CA’s letter where kilometres decide lakhs. For you: For your JD landowner partners this is THE conversation: many Ranga Reddy parcels sit inside Hyderabad’s 8 km band — urban, taxable — while one village further out is exempt. Knowing which side of the line a family’s land falls (and flagging 54B’s two-year farming condition early) makes you the developer who saved them lakhs before the deal even signed. 2026-10-02|ls-nri-guide: NRI guide to buying land in India: rules, restrictions, and what to know Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: NRI Guide to Buying Land in India: Rules, Restrictions, and What to Know Before You Invest — 1acre.in Key Highlights Residential and commercial property: NRIs buy freely — no cap, no RBI approval. Agricultural land, farmhouses and plantations: banned under FEMA, with three narrow exceptions. Repatriating sale money depends on FEMA rules, where the purchase money came from, and tax compliance. Long-term gains (held 24+ months) now taxed at 12.5% WITHOUT indexation — and NRIs miss the grandfathering relief residents got. Buying from abroad is an information problem: due diligence must happen BEFORE the wire, not after. Who counts as an NRI here The definitions run through FEMA, 1999. An NRI is an Indian citizen living abroad — Indian passport overseas. An OCI is a foreign citizen of Indian origin — foreign passport, Indian roots. For property purchases the two follow essentially identical rules, so everything below applies to both. What NRIs can and cannot buy Freely: apartments, villas, houses, offices, shops — residential and commercial, any number, no RBI approval. Never: agricultural land, farmhouses, plantation property — a national ban, whatever the buyer’s income or country, and it covers every route: sale deed, agreement to sell, or any indirect structure trying to dress the purchase up. Why the farmland ban exists The restriction lives in FEMA’s capital-account framework — today the Non-debt Instruments Rules, 2019 plus the RBI Master Direction, not one neat section. The policy logic: farmland touches food security, and offshore money flooding in could distort prices and displace the people who actually work the land. RBI approval technically exists but is granted rarely, for genuine agricultural or public-interest cases — it is not an investment route. And breaking the rule is not a slap on the wrist: the transaction can be VOIDED, the Enforcement Directorate can step in, and penalties can reach three times the value. The three exceptions Inheritance — the common path: an NRI can inherit farmland from a resident Indian (or from another NRI with RBI clearance), and can later sell it — but only to a resident Indian. Gift from a specified relative — allowed if the giver is a RESIDENT Indian who qualifies as a specified relative under FEMA; NRI-to-NRI farmland gifting is barred. Prior ownership — farmland you owned while resident stays yours after your status changes; the ban bites only on NEW acquisitions. In all three cases, sending the eventual sale money abroad is not automatic — RBI guidance and tax compliance govern it. The buying process, step by step 1) Confirm eligibility — your NRI/OCI status, and that the property is residential/commercial, not agricultural or plantation. 2) Shortlist RERA-registered projects and verify approvals with the authority. 3) Due diligence — 30-year title search plus EC, ruling out disputes, mortgages and legally non-transferable land. 4) Open the NRI account — NRE, NRO or FCNR; every rupee routes through it (cash is barred under FEMA and tax law alike). 5) Execute a PoA if you will not attend — embassy-attested or apostilled in Hague-convention countries, then stamped in India before use. 6) Sign the agreement on stamp paper with a payment schedule; register within four months. 7) Transfer funds and KEEP the Foreign Inward Remittance Certificate. 8) Pay stamp duty at the state’s rate. 9) Register the sale deed — in person or via the PoA holder — this is the ownership proof. 10) Afterwards: file tax on any rent, and keep records seven years. Definition — NRE / NRO / FCNR: the three NRI bank accounts. NRE holds foreign earnings (fully repatriable), NRO holds Indian earnings (repatriation capped), FCNR holds foreign-currency deposits. WHICH account funded the purchase decides how freely the sale money can leave later. Repatriation — getting money out later From an NRO account, up to USD 1 million per financial year can go abroad, subject to tax compliance. Property bought with FOREIGN funds via NRE: full repatriation of sale proceeds, for up to two residential properties; beyond two, the money joins the USD-1-million pipeline. Bought with NRO (India-earned) money: capped and paperwork-heavy. The lesson runs backwards in time: the repatriation freedom you want at EXIT is decided by the account you use at ENTRY. Example: Two NRIs each sell a Hyderabad flat for ₹2 crore. One bought via NRE with dollars — proceeds wire out cleanly. The other bought with NRO rupees — the same money now queues under the annual cap with Forms 15CA/15CB. Identical flats; the funding route made the difference. Documents you will need Identity: passport (with OCI card if applicable), PAN, proof of overseas residence. Property: title deed with 30-year history, EC, regulatory approvals, and for completed buildings the approved plan and occupancy certificate. Transaction: NRI-account statements, the FIRC, the attested PoA if buying in absentia, and Forms 15CA/15CB where remittances abroad cross ₹5 lakh a year. Tax obligations TDS turns on who SELLS: buy from a resident and TDS is the small 1% over ₹50 lakh; buy from another NRI and TDS applies at much higher rates regardless of value. Capital gains: property held over 24 months is long-term, taxed at 12.5% — and NRIs do NOT get the grandfathered indexation relief residents kept, so old purchases can carry surprisingly large taxable gains. Rent earned in India is taxed in India (standard deduction applies); tax treaties usually let you credit Indian tax against the home-country bill. Buying from a distance — the real risk The hardest part of absentee buying is the gap between what a listing claims and what the land is. Map overlays and verified survey numbers narrow that gap — classification, zoning, boundary, location — before you wire an advance or fly in. But no map reads a title chain, catches a forged deed, or gives FEMA and tax advice: a property lawyer and a tax advisor who handle NRI transactions remain non-negotiable, because a wrong classification does not just lose money — it can void the transaction. Quick answers (FAQ) Can an NRI buy restricted or assigned land? No — the assigned-land bans apply on top of FEMA. Any cap on how many properties? No cap on residential/commercial ownership; repatriation rules differ beyond two. Buy without visiting India? Yes — via a properly attested and stamped PoA. Sell inherited farmland? Yes, but only to a resident Indian. What if an NRI buys farmland in breach? Transaction voidable, ED proceedings, penalty up to 3× the value. Bottom line The rules are clear on paper and unforgiving in practice. Confirm the land’s classification BEFORE committing, route every payment through the right NRI account, and put a lawyer and tax advisor on the file — the two costs that are always cheaper than the mistake. For you: NRI money is a major buyer pool for Hyderabad plots — and every NRI buyer’s first fear is exactly this lesson. A venture that hands NRI buyers a ready file (residential classification proof, RERA number, PoA template, TDS guidance) converts that fear into sales. Also: never let a broker pitch your FARM plots to NRI buyers — that deal voids itself. Original Deccan Ledger lesson; full source article on 1acre.in (links above). The story, explained from zero — fact by fact S1 · The gazette notification A gazette notification issued 2 October 2026 by Telangana's Municipal Administration and Urban Development (MA&UD) department brought the Core Urban Region (Integrated Governance) Act, 2026 into legal force, repealing the Greater Hyderabad Municipal Corporation (GHMC) Act of 1955. Plain English: a nearly 70-year-old law governing how Hyderabad is run has been formally retired and replaced, effective today's date in the story. Mechanics: a gazette notification is the final administrative step that makes a passed, assented law actually operative on the ground — distinct from the Assembly passing it or the Governor signing it, both of which happened weeks earlier. S2 · What the CURE Act actually is The Act creates one unified governance framework — the "Core Urban Region," extending up to the Outer Ring Road (ORR) — for three separate municipal corporations: GHMC, Cyberabad Municipal Corporation (CMC) and Malkajgiri Municipal Corporation (MMC), together covering roughly 1.30 crore people, about a third of Telangana's population. Plain English: instead of three civic bodies each running on their own, there is now one law and one apex structure tying them together. Mechanics: CMC and MMC were only created in February 2026 by splitting the old, larger GHMC area into three; CURE is the first law written specifically to govern all three together rather than retrofitting the 1955 Act onto a three-way split it was never designed for. S3 · The headline change: property tax moves from rent to market value The Act replaces the Annual Rental Value (ARV) system — tax based on a property's assumed monthly rent — with a Capital Value System (CVS), under which tax is calculated as a percentage of the government's market/registration value of the property. Plain English: your tax bill used to be based on a notional, often outdated guess at what rent your property could fetch; now it will be based on what the government says your property is actually worth to buy. Numbers: one search-aggregated source (not independently fetch-confirmed) puts the new CVS rates at 0.15% of capital value for residential buildings and 0.75% for non-residential/commercial — flagged as partially verified, found via one aggregation, not a second independent fetch. S4 · Two different start dates for two different kinds of property CVS applies immediately, from 2 October 2026, to newly constructed properties being assessed for the first time; properties already assessed under the old ARV system move to CVS only from the start of the next financial year, 1 April 2027. Plain English: if you're building something new, the new, higher tax basis applies to you right away; if you already own an assessed property, you have roughly 17 months before the switch reaches you. Incentives: this phased rollout is a classic way to avoid an immediate, universal tax shock while still locking in the new system's eventual reach. S5 · The scale of the expected increase Multiple outlets, including Deccan Chronicle, frame the effect as property tax potentially "doubling" for many owners once fully phased in. Plain English: this is not a cosmetic change — outlets covering it consistently expect a large jump in actual rupee terms for many properties, especially ones whose rental valuation has sat unchanged for years while market prices rose. Flag: a specific worked example (a 1,000 sq ft Jubilee Hills flat allegedly going from ₹5,540/year to roughly ₹12,333/year) appeared in search-aggregated results tracing to a single outlet's analysis piece; it could not be independently re-confirmed via a direct fetch, so treat the direction (large increase) as well-corroborated and the specific rupee figures as unverified. S6 · The cap that softens the blow: 10%, not 20% The CURE Bill originally proposed capping any single year's tax-revision increase at 20%; during the Assembly debate on 12 September 2026, Minister D. Sridhar Babu announced the cap had been reduced to 10%, "with the permission of the Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy." Plain English: even though your property's true new tax liability under CVS might be much higher than your old ARV bill, the law stops your tax bill from jumping by more than 10% in any one year — so a doubling happens gradually over several years, not in one shock. Mechanics: this amendment was announced on the floor during debate itself, not pre-drafted into the Bill as introduced. S7 · A new stick behind the Occupancy Certificate The Act bars municipal corporations from providing electricity, drinking water or sewerage connections to any building lacking an Occupancy Certificate (OC), and makes any official who releases such a service anyway liable for disciplinary action, including removal from service. Plain English: getting your power and water connected informally before your building has a full, final OC is meant to become much harder, because the official who approves it now personally risks their job. Flag: the exact statutory section number and the disciplinary procedure (which authority investigates, appeal rights) could not be confirmed from available reporting. S8 · A separate, more contested clause: disconnection for a builder's unpaid dues A related provision, opposed by developer and resident groups, lets corporations disconnect water, sewerage or power to an already-occupied building if its builder/developer has outstanding dues owed to the government. Plain English: this is a different mechanism from S7 above — here, people already living in a completed building could lose services over a payment dispute between their builder and the government, not their own default. Incentives: critics argue this effectively holds homebuyers hostage to enforce builder compliance, since the people who can least fix the underlying dues (the residents) bear the actual consequence. S9 · The legislative journey: four-plus hours of debate, several parties objecting The Telangana Legislative Assembly passed the CURE Bill by voice vote on 12 September 2026, on the fifth day of its monsoon session, after a debate lasting over four hours; BJP, AIMIM and CPI members raised objections, while BRS — per one unverified search synthesis — did not substantively participate because its MLAs had reportedly been suspended for the remainder of that session. Plain English: this was not a quiet, uncontested bill — multiple opposition parties pushed back hard on the floor, even though the ruling Congress had the numbers to pass it by voice vote anyway. Flag: the specific claim that BRS MLAs were suspended during this debate could not be verified against a named, primary source and should be treated as unconfirmed. S10 · What the opposition specifically objected to BJP MLA Palvai Harish Babu argued the law would curtail elected mayors' and corporators' powers while concentrating authority in a CM-chaired apex council, creating "scope for corruption," and separately criticised the ARV-to-CVS tax shift and HYDRAA's expanded powers; AIMIM floor leader Akbaruddin Owaisi sought referral to a Select Committee for clause-by-clause scrutiny and warned the Bill could face legal challenges in court; CPI members registered general "reservations and apprehensions." Plain English: the objections ran on two tracks — "this will cost residents more money" (the tax shift) and "this takes power away from elected local representatives and gives it to unelected, centrally-appointed bodies" (the governance structure). Flag: no CPI MLA is named with a specific quote in available reporting. S11 · The Governor's role, and a bypassed request to reconsider Public policy expert Donthi Narasimha Reddy wrote to Governor Shiv Pratap Shukla on 16 September 2026 urging him to return the Bill to the Assembly for reconsideration, citing concerns about the CURE Apex Governance Council's powers; the Governor did not act on this request and instead gave his assent on 22 September 2026. Plain English: there was a specific, named attempt to stop or slow this law after it passed the Assembly but before it became operative law, and it did not succeed. Mechanics: a Governor can return an ordinary bill (not a money bill) to the Assembly for reconsideration, but is not obliged to; here, assent followed six days after the request, suggesting it was not taken up. S12 · Objection from residents during the consultation window, before any of this Before the Bill was even introduced, the government released a draft CURE Bill for public consultation from roughly 5 to 24 July 2026, receiving over 4,000 suggestions and incorporating 70 changes before introduction; separately, over 3,000 residents are reported to have formally objected specifically to the capital-value taxation approach. Plain English: this was not a law sprung on the public with no warning — there was a real, if ultimately only partially effective, consultation process, and a large number of residents specifically flagged the tax mechanism as their concern months before it took effect. Glossary — every term, simply Annual Rental Value (ARV) The old property-tax basis: your tax was calculated as a percentage of the rent your property was assumed to be able to fetch each year — a notional figure, not what anyone actually pays, and one that can stay unchanged for years even as real prices rise. Capital Value System (CVS) The new property-tax basis: tax is calculated as a small percentage of the property's government-assessed market value — the same value used to work out stamp duty when a property is sold. Example: Mumbai already uses a similar system, where a recent revision produced roughly a 15–16% average tax increase for most properties. Gazette notification The official government publication that makes a law legally operative on a stated date — the last of several steps after an Assembly passes a bill and a Governor signs it. Occupancy Certificate (OC) A certificate confirming a completed building matches its approved plan and is safe to occupy; without it, a building technically cannot legally be lived in, though in practice informal workarounds (getting power/water connected anyway) have been common — exactly what this Act tries to close off. Trifurcation Splitting one body into three — here, dividing the old, larger GHMC into today's smaller GHMC plus the newly created Cyberabad and Malkajgiri corporations, done in February 2026, ahead of and separate from the CURE Act itself. Select Committee referral A legislative process where a bill is sent to a smaller group of MLAs for detailed, clause-by-clause review before the full House votes — AIMIM asked for this on CURE and did not get it; the Bill instead went straight to a floor vote. 74th Constitutional Amendment / Part IX-A (Articles 243P, 243Q, 243W) The constitutional provisions guaranteeing elected local self-government (municipalities, their powers and functions) in India — the legal basis critics point to when arguing that CURE's CM-chaired apex council and specialised unelected authorities may excessively dilute elected mayors' and corporators' constitutional role. Ready Reckoner rate (Mumbai comparison) Maharashtra's name for the government-published market-value benchmark used in Mumbai's own capital-value property tax system — the direct precedent Telangana's CVS is modelled on in spirit, though Hyderabad uses its own locally-published guideline/market values instead. The backstory — how we got here 14 Feb 1956 Hyderabad Municipal Corporations Act, 1955 receives Presidential assent (Act No. II of 1956) — the law CURE now replaces. 1960 Hyderabad and Secunderabad Corporations merge into one Hyderabad Municipal Corporation. 2007 12 surrounding municipalities merged in; entity renamed Greater Hyderabad Municipal Corporation (GHMC); Act renamed the GHMC Act, 1955. 11 Feb 2026 GHMC trifurcated: Cyberabad and Malkajgiri Municipal Corporations formally created; ₹500 crore allocated to each. ~5–24 Jul 2026 Draft CURE Bill released for public consultation; 4,000+ suggestions received, 70 changes made; 3,000+ residents separately object specifically to the capital-value tax approach. 12 Sep 2026 Assembly passes the CURE Bill by voice vote after 4+ hours of debate; 20% tax-cap proposal reduced to 10% on the floor; BJP, AIMIM, CPI object. 16 Sep 2026 Donthi Narasimha Reddy writes to Governor Shiv Pratap Shukla urging the Bill be returned for reconsideration. 22 Sep 2026 Governor Shukla gives assent; the Bill becomes law. 2 Oct 2026 Today: gazette notification brings the Act into force; CVS applies immediately to newly-assessed properties. 1 Apr 2027 Future: CVS extends to all existing, already-assessed properties. The deeper pattern: this is the second major structural step in under eight months — first the quiet administrative trifurcation of GHMC into three corporations (February 2026), now the legal and fiscal unification of those same three bodies under one tax system and one apex council (October 2026). What a long-time Hyderabad civic-affairs watcher knows that a first-time reader doesn't: the trifurcation and CURE are two halves of the same reorganisation, separated by about eight months, and the property-tax change was the part of CURE the public consultation process generated the most pushback on — yet it passed essentially as planned, softened only by the 20%-to-10% cap, not reversed. So what — stakes and consequences Winners: the state and municipal exchequer, which gains a tax base tied to rising market values instead of frozen rental assumptions (one unconfirmed figure put CURE-area corporations' current property-tax collection at roughly ₹2,501 crore, with Cyberabad topping the list); and the new specialised institutions — the CM-chaired CURE Apex Governance Council, an empowered HYDRAA, and new bodies like a Disaster Management Authority and Climate Action Cell — all of which gain fresh statutory standing and, in HYDRAA's case, its own dedicated police-station structure. Losers, or at-risk parties: existing homeowners facing a potential near-doubling of property tax once CVS fully phases in (softened, not eliminated, by the 10% annual cap); developers facing both tighter OC-linked connection rules and the more contested builder-dues disconnection clause that can penalise already-moved-in residents for a builder's unpaid government dues; and elected mayors, corporators and ward committees, whose statutory role critics argue is diluted relative to the new unelected, centrally-coordinated bodies — a tension with the 74th Constitutional Amendment's guarantee of elected local self-government that AIMIM's Akbaruddin Owaisi explicitly flagged as likely litigation grounds. Watch: (a) likely — continued lobbying from FGCC, CREDAI and resident associations over the next several months to soften or delay the 1 April 2027 extension of CVS to existing properties; (b) plausible — a constitutional legal challenge in the Telangana High Court citing Part IX-A (Articles 243P, 243Q, 243W) against the CURE Apex Governance Council's structure, though no such petition was confirmed filed as of this edition; (c) less likely but real — the builder-dues disconnection clause gets amended or diluted if enough resident backlash lands on sitting Congress MLAs before the 2027 switch-over. What this means for you: For Hyderabad/Telangana real estate: price every new project's post-handover carrying cost assuming full CVS-linked tax within a few years, not the old ARV figure, and get genuinely rigorous about Occupancy Certificates on every project — the informal-connection workaround this Act targets is exactly the kind of practice that can suddenly become a personal liability for the official who helped you, not just a paperwork delay for you. For business/investment generally: watch how the 10% annual cap performs as a political shock-absorber — a government can legislate a large structural change (near-doubling of a tax) and still make it politically survivable by spreading the pain across many budget years; that is a reusable playbook worth recognising elsewhere. The beginner mistake is treating "property tax goes up" as the whole story; the sharper expert read is that CURE is simultaneously a tax reform AND a governance-centralisation reform, and the second part is what is actually contested in court and in Assembly debate, not the first. The 20% that gives you 100% — your keep-forever map Telangana has retired the 70-year-old GHMC Act and replaced it with the CURE Act, which for the first time governs GHMC, Cyberabad and Malkajgiri Municipal Corporations — split from one another only in February 2026 — under one framework. The headline change is a shift from taxing Hyderabad-area property on notional rental value to taxing it on market value, expected to roughly double many bills over time but capped at a 10% increase per year after the originally-proposed 20% cap was softened on the Assembly floor. New properties feel this immediately (2 October 2026); existing ones get until 1 April 2027. A new disciplinary rule also closes the informal practice of connecting power and water to buildings without a final Occupancy Certificate. The law passed despite real opposition from BJP, AIMIM and CPI over both the tax shift and a parallel concern that it concentrates power in a CM-chaired council at the expense of elected mayors and ward committees — a tension that could yet produce a constitutional legal challenge. Five lessons worth keeping: A tax base tied to market value always eventually produces a bigger bill than one tied to a frozen notional figure — the mechanism, not the politics, decides that. Annual caps are a standard, effective way governments make a large structural tax change politically survivable — expect to see this pattern again elsewhere. Administrative reorganisation (trifurcation) and legal/fiscal unification (CURE) can be two separate steps months apart — always ask which stage a "reform" story is actually describing. A real public consultation process does not guarantee the most-objected-to provision gets dropped — it may only get capped or phased, as happened here. Whenever a law adds personal disciplinary liability for officials over a compliance step (like releasing a connection without an OC), treat every informal workaround you've relied on as newly fragile. 2026-10-03|ls-patta-vs-deed: The real difference between patta, sale deed, and title deed Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: The Real Difference Between Patta, Sale Deed, and Title Deed — 1acre.in Key Highlights Patta vs sale deed = tax record vs transfer of ownership. Only one moves title. A patta SUPPORTS an ownership claim; it does not create one — no court treats it as proof of title. “Title deed” is not a document at all — it is the category term for the registered instruments behind your ownership chain. When patta and deed disagree, the registered deed generally prevails — but the mismatch still blocks resale and loans until mutation fixes it. Revenue records wear different names across states; the administrative job is the same. Why the difference matters Three documents, three different questions. A patta answers: whose name does the revenue department hold against this survey number? A sale deed answers: did a legal transfer occur? A title deed answers: is the ownership chain behind that transfer clean? Confusing them is not a vocabulary slip — it decides which paper a buyer trusts when the papers conflict. What a patta records — and does not Issued by the revenue department, not a court: landholder’s name, extent, survey number. Its function is administrative — tax assessment and revenue tracking. Real uses: banks ask for it before lending against land; it supports a possession claim in a dispute; it confirms the parcel exists in state records under a stated name. What it does NOT do is create ownership — courts have consistently held revenue records are evidence of possession, not conclusive proof of title. (Telangana’s pattadar passbook, Maharashtra’s 7/12, Karnataka’s RTC — different names, same administrative job.) Why the registered sale deed carries the most weight The deed is the instrument that MOVES ownership; registration is what gives it force. Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act: any sale of immovable property worth ₹100 or more requires a registered instrument — which, at that threshold, means EVERY land sale in India; the folk belief that registration only applies above some higher value is simply wrong. Section 17 of the Registration Act makes the registration compulsory; and Section 49 delivers the consequence — an unregistered document that required registration cannot even be received as evidence of the transaction. Registration also feeds the public record every future EC draws from: the paper trail exists because the statute compels it. “Title deed” is a category, not a certificate No office in India issues a document titled “title deed”. The term describes whichever registered instruments TOGETHER establish you hold the property free of competing claims: your registered sale deed plus the deeds behind it — earlier sales, partitions, gifts — back to the Mother Deed that first established ownership. When a bank asks for “title documents”, it wants that SET. And a title deed’s strength is borrowed: exactly as strong as the registered instruments standing behind it, and no stronger. Definition — Mother Deed: the earliest traceable document that established ownership of the parcel — the root of the chain. Every later deed inherits its validity from this root; a defect there flows down through everything. The three compared Aspect Patta / revenue record Sale deed Title deed Issued by Revenue department Executed by parties, registered at SRO Not issued — the chain of registered instruments Function Tax + revenue tracking Transfers ownership Establishes the clean chain Legal weight Evidence of possession The operative instrument As strong as the deeds composing it Buyer’s use Cross-check + loan requirement The document you actually acquire by What your advocate traces 30 years back When patta and deed disagree The registered deed generally prevails — ownership does not wait for the revenue record to catch up. But the mismatch still does practical damage: a patta in the previous owner’s name stalls your RESALE (the next buyer’s advocate flags it), stalls a LOAN (the bank matches patta name against deed), and can send tax demands to the wrong person for years. The correction is MUTATION: file with the revenue authority, attaching the registered deed, EC, identity proof and the previous revenue record. Fix it because it blocks your next transaction — not because your ownership depends on it. Example: A buyer holds a clean 2021 registered deed but never mutated; the passbook still names the seller. In 2025 the resale buyer’s bank refuses sanction on the name mismatch, and the deal waits months for a mutation that would have taken weeks back in 2021. The deed was always enough for OWNERSHIP — never enough for the next transaction. Your document checklist ☐ Start with the registered sale deed — the heaviest of the three. ☐ Trace the chain behind it to the Mother Deed, watching for gaps. ☐ Compare patta vs deed on name, extent, survey number. ☐ File mutation if the revenue record lags. ☐ Pull a separate EC for hidden loans and claims. Quick answers (FAQ) Does a patta prove ownership? No — it supports possession; the registered deed chain proves title. Is a title deed the same as a sale deed? The sale deed is usually its main component; the title deed is the whole chain. Can I sell if the patta still shows the previous owner? Legally the deed lets you — practically, mutate first or watch buyers walk. Can an EC replace a patta? No — they answer different questions (registered transactions vs revenue holding); a full check uses both. Bottom line Deed for ownership, patta for the record, chain for confidence — verify all three and make them agree before money moves. Where they disagree, the deed wins the law and the mismatch loses you the deal. For you: Use the three-question frame in every negotiation: whose name does Dharani hold (patta)? did a registered transfer occur (deed)? is the chain clean to the root (title)? A seller strong on one and vague on the others has told you where to dig. And keep your own ventures’ trinity aligned — deed, passbook, mutation — plot by plot; it is what “clear-title developer” means in practice. It does not prove ownership — that is the title deed’s job. The EC validates; it does not replace. Its blind spot is everything unregistered: private loans, informal partitions, unregistered agreements, most litigation. A “clean” (Nil) EC can simply mean the search ran on the wrong number or window. Read it WITH the title chain and the ground — alone, it leaves gaps a buyer can walk straight into. What an EC actually shows A government-issued log from the SRO of every registered event on the property in your chosen period: sales, mortgages, gifts, releases, leases — with owners as they appear in deeds, the property description, and document numbers and dates for each entry. It has become India’s shorthand for title verification: banks refuse loans without a clear one; lawyers start every search here. Why an EC is not proof of ownership The single most important sentence in this lesson: the EC shows registered TRANSACTION history; OWNERSHIP is proved by the title deed and the chain behind it. Think of the EC as the property’s credit report — what happened on record — not its birth certificate. What the EC misses entirely Only registered documents enter it. So these never appear: oral family settlements; informal partitions between siblings; unregistered agreements to sell; private loans through unregistered mortgages — including the very common deposit-of-title-deeds mortgage with a bank; and court cases, unless officially recorded at the SRO. Definition — Equitable mortgage (deposit of title deeds): a loan created by handing the original deeds to a lender. No registration, no EC entry — which is why sighting the ORIGINALS is a due-diligence step no certificate replaces. Example: Spotless 30-year EC; seller’s originals “with his brother”. More often than not the originals are with a bank, against a loan the EC cannot see. The absence of originals is the loudest entry the EC never prints. EC vs the other property documents Document What it proves What it does NOT prove Encumbrance Certificate Registered transaction/liability history for a period Ownership; unregistered deals; undisclosed litigation Title / sale deed Legal ownership and its transfer to the holder Freedom from hidden liabilities — the EC’s job Mutation certificate The property’s entry in revenue/tax records Legal ownership — mutation is a tax record Property tax receipts Taxes paid; possession exercised Clear title or absence of disputes The classic misreadings The mortgage with no release deed — the property may still be pledged; if the loan was never cleared the lender’s rights survive your purchase. The Nil EC celebrated too early — Form 16 (nil) may mean genuinely clean, or wrong survey number, or wrong classification; a clean result is a prompt to verify WHY it is clean, against pahani / extract / patta. The unexplained jump — ownership hopping from one name to a third with no visible link; that missing link is precisely what a careful read catches. Definition — Form 15 / Form 16: the two faces of an EC in the southern states: Form 15 lists the registered entries found; Form 16 is the nil-encumbrance certificate saying the search found nothing in the window. What to check alongside the EC The sale deed and title chain; mutation entries; tax receipts; a physical survey against documented boundaries; and an independent litigation check through court records. Window: minimum 13 years, ideally 30 — the certificate only reflects the period actually searched. Pre-purchase checklist ☐ EC for 13–30 years, survey number matching the deed exactly. ☐ Nil results cross-checked against revenue records before celebrating. ☐ Every mortgage entry paired with its release deed. ☐ No unexplained gaps between names in the chain. ☐ EC read TOGETHER with deed, mutation and tax receipts. ☐ Lawyer review when anything looks inconsistent. Quick answers (FAQ) Does an EC prove ownership? No — it validates the title story; the deed chain tells it. Can an unregistered loan appear? No — that is the blind spot; hunt it through the originals. Can litigation be missing from an EC? Yes, routinely — run the court search separately. Is a clean EC always good news? It is a question wearing good news’s clothes: why is it clean? Bottom line The EC is a necessary check, never a complete one — what was registered, not who owns. Pair it with the chain, the mutation record and the ground, and its silences stop being traps. For you: Two reflexes for every deal: originals sighted, and the EC read line-by-line by you — the entry that matters is often a release deed that never came, sitting quietly in year 14 of a 30-year window. 2026-10-04|ls-agri-to-resi: How to convert agricultural land to residential property Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: How to Convert Agricultural Land to Residential Property — 1acre.in Key Highlights Agricultural land must usually be CONVERTED before residential construction is legal on it. Approval depends on the master plan, zoning and state land-use law — not on willingness to pay. Green belts, protected agricultural zones, forests and environmentally restricted land often cannot be converted at any price. The order comes from the competent planning or revenue authority, with documents and a site inspection. Buying land “already converted”? Verify the order is VALID and unexpired — a lapsed conversion reverts the land to agricultural. Agricultural vs residential land: the real difference Agricultural land is meant for farming, and its registration, taxation and transfer rules all follow from that purpose. Converted land costs more per square yard — but it carries the legal standing you need to build, raise a home loan, or sell to someone who will. The premium is not decoration; it is the difference between a plot and a field. What the law actually requires Start with the MASTER PLAN, not the application form — this is where most people get the sequence backwards. Formal conversion approval from the competent planning or revenue authority is required before agricultural land can legally host residential construction, and that approval must align with the master plan zone, the zoning classification, and the state’s land-revenue statutes. Two hard truths follow: where the plan already designates the land residential, conversion is not discretionary — it should be granted; where the plan marks the zone green belt, forest or agriculture-protection, conversion is simply NOT AVAILABLE. No fee fixes a blocking zone. Definition — Master plan: the government’s long-term land-use map for a region — which areas are residential, commercial, industrial, green. In conversion matters it outranks everything: the plan decides what is possible; the application only executes it. Documents you will need ☐ Title deed and the 30-year chain of title. ☐ Updated land-record extract — registered deed, 7/12, patta, or your state’s equivalent (pattadar passbook in Telangana). ☐ Survey sketch, master plan extract, and an EC. ☐ NOCs from agriculture, town planning, forest or water-resources departments where applicable. Getting the file right the FIRST time saves months of back-and-forth. The step-by-step process 1) Pull the master plan extract; confirm the zone permits residential use. 2) File the application with the revenue or planning authority for your state and zone. 3) Pay the conversion fee — assessed on area, location and proposed use. 4) Site inspection: an official verifies the land matches the application. 5) Receive the conversion order; the land record is updated. 6) READ THE CONDITIONS on pages two and three — they decide whether the order stays alive. 7) Apply for building-plan sanction from the local body before any construction starts — conversion permits the USE; the sanction permits the BUILDING. Common challenges The zone itself blocking the change — no application can convert green-belt, forest or protection-zone land. Delays or rejection from incomplete files, missing NOCs, or mismatches found at inspection. And the quiet one: conversion orders that LAPSE because construction timelines or conditions went unmet — leaving the land agricultural despite a framed approval on the wall. Example: A buyer pays a premium for a “converted” plot with a 2019 order. Condition 4 on page two required construction to commence within three years; nothing was built. The order lapsed in 2022 — the parcel is agricultural again, and the premium bought paper. One reading of the conditions would have repriced the deal. Best practices before you start Master plan zone first; then road access, water and soil. A short consultation with a local surveyor costs less than discovering a blocking issue after the fee is paid. And engage someone who knows THAT district’s revenue office — procedures genuinely differ between neighbouring districts. Quick answers (FAQ) Is conversion mandatory before building a house? Generally yes — building on unconverted agricultural land invites demolition and denies you sanction, loans and clean resale. Who approves? The competent revenue or planning authority (RDO/Collector-side in Telangana, with HMDA/DTCP layers for layouts). Can any land be converted if I pay? No — the zone decides; money cannot move a green belt. Does an order expire? Yes — it is conditional and time-bound; verify validity when buying “converted” land. Can NRIs apply? For land they lawfully hold (e.g. inherited) — subject to the same zoning rules. If I skip conversion? Unauthorised use: penalties, demolition risk, no sanction, and a discount when you sell. Bottom line Conversion is a sequence, not a fee: zone first, statute second, payment last — and the order you receive is a living document with conditions and an expiry. Read it like a contract, because it is one. For you: This is the machinery of your margin: farmland in, NA/DTCP-approved plots out. Your edge is the SEQUENCE discipline — verify the master-plan zone before the land is even priced, and when buying “converted” parcels from others, audit the order’s conditions and dates like a bank would. 2026-10-04|ls-poa-rules: Power of Attorney for land: rules, risks, and what holds up in court Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: Power of Attorney for Land: Rules, Risks, and What Actually Holds Up in Court — 1acre.in Key Highlights A PoA authorises someone to ACT for you — sign, register, manage, negotiate. It can never hand over ownership. Suraj Lamp (Supreme Court, 2011) settled it: a PoA is not a title-transfer instrument; Shakeel Ahmed (2023) confirmed old GPA chains get no pass. A PoA normally DIES with the principal (Section 201) — except where the agent holds a real interest in the property (Section 202). Registration is mandatory whenever a PoA creates an interest in land, is marked irrevocable, or empowers sale/gift/transfer. Stamp duty turns on the relationship: close family pay nominal rates; unrelated buyers/developers face conveyance-level charges. What a PoA actually does for land One person — the principal — authorises another — the agent — to act on their behalf: signing agreements, handling Sub-Registrar paperwork, managing tenants, negotiating a sale. Representative authority only. The persistent confusion is treating a PoA as a stand-in for a sale — it is not and cannot be: under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, only a REGISTERED SALE DEED transfers title to immovable property. GPA vs SPA: picking the instrument A General PoA grants sweeping authority — suited to an NRI overseeing property across years and distance, but broad authority is hard to police, and if the agent oversteps, the very breadth makes the overstep harder to prove. A Special PoA is built for ONE job and expires when it is done. For land, advocates lean SPA: narrow scope, less room for misuse, cleaner record. What the Supreme Court has said Suraj Lamp (2011) : the “GPA sale” — the once-common practice of selling property via GPA + agreement + will, skipping the sale deed and its stamp duty — transfers NO title. Shakeel Ahmed (2023) : confirmed the principle applies to old chains too — decades-old GPA transactions do not ripen into ownership with time. If your seller’s ownership story runs through a GPA instead of a registered deed, there is no ownership in the story. Example: A Shamshabad plot is offered cheap: the “owner” bought it in 2008 “on GPA” from the recorded owner and has possession ever since. Under Suraj Lamp he owns nothing — only the recorded owner (or their heirs) can convey. The fix, if everyone is alive and willing: a proper registered sale deed from the true owner now, with duty paid. Without that, the plot is unbuyable at any discount. The five classic PoA risks 1) Revoked but presented as valid — an unregistered cancellation shows no outward sign, so a revoked PoA can still deceive a third party. 2) Death of the principal — agency ends automatically under Section 201; anything signed after is void — except the narrow Section 202 case where the agent holds a genuine interest in the property itself. 3) Tangled chains of sub-authority — each PoA granting power to the next makes true ownership harder to trace; buyers inherit disputes they never saw. 4) Self-dealing — an agent selling to HIMSELF is valid only if the PoA explicitly permits it; otherwise a breach of fiduciary duty. 5) Missing registration — where a PoA permits sale, gift or transfer, registration at the sub-registrar is not optional; skipping it guts the document’s standing. Definition — Section 202 (Contract Act): the exception that makes a PoA survive the principal’s death: when the agent has a real INTEREST in the property (say, money already advanced against it), the authority is coupled with that interest and does not lapse. Everything else dies with the principal. Registration, stamp duty, validity Registration is mandatory when the PoA creates an interest in land, is marked irrevocable, or empowers sale/gift/transfer; a PoA limited to rent collection follows lighter rules. Stamp duty follows the relationship : close family typically nominal; an unrelated buyer or developer holding a sale-empowering PoA can face conveyance-level duty — precisely to kill the GPA-sale dodge. NRIs : execute before the Indian mission (or apostille in Hague-convention countries) and stamp within three months of the document reaching India. How to verify a land PoA before acting on it ☐ The PoA names the exact survey number, the exact act, and a duration. ☐ Registered, where the sale/irrevocable/interest test applies. ☐ A revocation clause built in from day one. ☐ The principal INDEPENDENTLY confirmed as owner — in the state land record, not the PoA’s own recitals. ☐ The principal confirmed ALIVE (for a Section 201 document, this is not a formality). ☐ EC pulled — showing any PoA, mortgage or transaction already registered against the parcel. ☐ The land itself transferable — no assigned/prohibited/acquisition taint, because no PoA overrides a land-law restriction. Quick answers (FAQ) Can a PoA be used to SELL land? An agent under a valid, registered, sale-empowering PoA can EXECUTE a sale deed for the owner — but the PoA itself never makes anyone an owner. Does calling it “irrevocable” make it irrevocable? No — the label doesn’t; only a genuine Section 202 interest does. What if the principal dies? Authority ends; post-death signatures are void (Section 202 excepted). Stamp duty? Relationship-dependent — nominal for close family, conveyance-level for unrelated sale-empowered holders. Bottom line A PoA is a tool for ACTING at a distance, not for owning. Verify the principal, the registration, the scope and the land’s own transferability — and treat any ownership chain that runs through a GPA as a chain with a missing link. For you: Two rules for your desk. Buying: any parcel whose chain contains a “GPA sale” is unpriced risk — either the true owner signs a fresh registered deed or you pass. Structuring your own JDs: the development GPA you take from landowners should be SPECIAL, scoped to the project, registered, with the JDA’s reversion clause mirrored in it — broad GPAs frighten landowners and courts alike. The story, explained from zero — sentence by sentence S1 · The core deal HILT lets an industrial landowner inside the ORR swap their factory plot’s legal land-use label to residential or commercial, provided they pay the government a conversion fee and physically move the factory itself beyond the ORR. Plain English: think of a shop owner on a busy market street being allowed to pay the municipality a fee and move the actual shop to the outskirts, in exchange for turning the shop’s old plot into something far more valuable, like flats or offices. Mechanics: the owner applies via the TG-iPASS/HILTP portal, pays a one-time Development Impact Fee calculated off the Sub-Registrar Office (SRO) land value, the land-use label changes from “Industrial” to “Multi-Use Zone,” and the unit must relocate beyond the ORR within a set timeframe. Incentives: the owner wants to cash in on land that is now worth vastly more as housing/office land than as factory land; the government wants both a lump-sum fee today and polluting units pushed out of a growing city. Numbers: 9,292 eligible acres across 22 estates; fee is 30% or 50% of SRO value depending on abutting road width. S2 · When it actually started This is not a brand-new announcement — the government notified the policy in a formal order back in November 2025. Plain English: a Government Order (G.O.) is the official birth certificate of a scheme; nothing is legally live until a paper like this is signed. Mechanics: G.O. Ms. No. 27, dated 22 November 2025, issued by the Industries & Commerce Department, formally created HILTP. Numbers: 22 Nov 2025. S3 · The first attempt flopped Factory owners did not rush to apply, so the initial 2026 deadline arrived with a disappointingly thin set of applications. Plain English: like a retailer announcing a big discount and barely any customers showing up. Incentives: owners weigh relocation cost and disruption against the conversion windfall; where relocation costs or uncertainty look larger than the gain, they simply sit out. S4 · The do-over Rather than letting the scheme quietly die, the government reopened the application window on 1 August 2026. Mechanics: a second window, with some early-filer benefits (old SRO rates, lower upfront fee share) still attached for those who had moved early. S5 · This week’s scorecard As of the first week of October 2026, the cumulative tally across both windows stands at about 193 applications covering roughly 450 acres. Numbers: 450 of 4,740 acres — under 10% of the convertible ceiling taken up after nearly a year of the scheme being open.
